articles.title: Vivek Ramaswamy to Nithya Raman: 4 Indian-origin candidates eye historic firsts in US elections 2026
articles.summary: Americans on Tuesday vote in elections that could determine the balance of power in Congress and shape politics across the country.
articles.body: Americans on Tuesday vote in elections that could determine the balance of power in Congress and shape politics across the country. Amid the wider electoral battle, four candidates of Indian origin are chasing milestones that could expand the representation of the Indian-American community in public office.Republican Vivek Ramaswamy is running for governor of Ohio, Democrat Nithya Raman is challenging incumbent Karen Bass for mayor of Los Angeles, Democrat Pooja Sethi is contesting a seat in the Texas House of Representatives, and Democrat Pia Dandiya is seeking election to the US House from Florida.The four contests differ in their political stakes, the offices involved and the issues facing voters. But each offers a glimpse into the growing presence of Indian Americans in US electoral politics.Here is what each candidate could achieve.Vivek Ramaswamy: A first Hindu governor?Vivek Ramaswamy could make history by becoming the first Indian-American governor of Ohio and the first Hindu governor in the United States.Born in Cincinnati to parents who immigrated from India, Ramaswamy grew up in a Hindu family. He studied at Harvard University before earning a law degree from Yale Law School and building a career in biotechnology and investment.He founded Roivant Sciences, a biopharmaceutical company, in 2014 and subsequently became a prominent conservative political commentator. His public profile grew during the 2024 presidential campaign, when he sought the Republican nomination before withdrawing and endorsing President Donald Trump.Ramaswamy became associated with Trump's efforts to reduce federal government spending and government bureaucracy. He eventually turned his attention to Ohio politics, winning the Republican nomination for governor in May 2026.He is facing Democrat Amy Acton, a physician and former director of the Ohio Department of Health. The winner will succeed Republican Governor Mike DeWine, who is term-limited.The contest is significant beyond Ramaswamy's background. Ohio has voted Republican in recent presidential elections, and the outcome will test whether Democrats can regain the governorship after nearly two decades without holding it.Ramaswamy's candidacy also challenges assumptions about the relationship between immigrant identity and political ideology. His Hindu heritage is distinct from the conservative Republican platform on which he is campaigning.Nithya Raman: Could Los Angeles get its first South Asian mayor?In California, urban planner and Los Angeles City Council member Nithya Raman is challenging incumbent Mayor Karen Bass in a contest that could make her the city's first South Asian mayor.Raman, who was born in India and moved to the US as a child, studied at Harvard University and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. Before entering electoral politics, she worked on urban planning and homelessness-related issues.She made political history in 2020 when she won a seat on the Los Angeles City Council, becoming the first South Asian to serve on the council and the first Asian-American woman to hold the position.Her work has focused on housing affordability, homelessness and improving city services. Those issues have also become central to her mayoral campaign, as Los Angeles continues to grapple with high housing costs and a persistent homelessness crisis.Bass, who is seeking re-election, has faced scrutiny over her administration's handling of homelessness and the city's response to the devastating Palisades fires in 2025.Raman has positioned herself as a candidate for change, while the contest has exposed divisions among Democrats over housing policy, policing and the direction of city government.The race is particularly notable because it is not a conventional contest between Republicans and Democrats. Los Angeles mayoral elections are officially nonpartisan, and both Bass and Raman are Democrats.A Raman victory would therefore be both a milestone for Indian representation and a test of whether voters want a different approach to governing one of America's largest cities.Pooja Sethi: A potential breakthrough in Texas politicsDemocrat Pooja Sethi is contesting Texas House District 47 against Republican Jennifer Mushtaler.According to election coverage, a victory would make Sethi the first Indian-American and the first Hindu elected to the Texas Legislature. The claim is significant in a state where immigration, education, reproductive rights and the role of government are recurring political flashpoints.Sethi is an immigration lawyer and former chair of the Travis County Democratic Party. Her professional experience has involved legal practice, political organising and community engagement.Her campaign has highlighted public education and affordability. She has advocated better funding for public schools, improved teacher pay and adequate support for students requiring special education. She also opposes school voucher policies that would direct public funds towards private education.The Texas House plays an important role in determining state policy, including education funding, taxation and public services. A seat in the legislature would give Sethi a direct role in shaping laws that affect millions of Texans.Her contest also illustrates how the political participation of Indian Americans extends beyond national elections. State legislatures often make decisions that have a more immediate impact on residents' daily lives than debates in Washington.However, Sethi's background alone will not determine the outcome. She faces a Republican opponent in a state where the party has substantial political strength, and the result will depend on voters' assessment of the candidates and their platforms.Pia Dandiya: A competitive race for CongressIn Florida, Democrat Pia Dandiya is running for the US House of Representatives from the 22nd Congressional District against Republican Casey Askar.Dandiya was born and raised in Palm Beach County to parents who immigrated from India. Her career has taken her through education, government and the private sector.She began as a teacher before becoming a high school principal. She subsequently served as a White House Fellow, working on domestic policy and education, and later worked at Apple on public-sector initiatives involving education and healthcare.Her campaign has made affordability a central issue, focusing on housing and insurance costs, healthcare, childcare and education. She has also called for government reforms and measures to address the influence of wealthy donors and lobbyists in politics.Dandiya's contest is among the closely watched congressional races in Florida. The state's mid-decade redistricting changed the boundaries of the 22nd District, making it more competitive than it was under its previous configuration.The seat has no incumbent in the 2026 election. Representative Lois Frankel, who previously held the district, is seeking re-election in the neighbouring 23rd District.Election forecasters have described the 22nd District as a toss-up, although some assessments give Republicans an advantage. Dandiya therefore faces a closely contested race in which campaign resources, turnout and voter concerns about the cost of living could prove decisive.A victory would add another Indian-American voice to Congress, but her candidacy should be understood primarily in the context of the district's political dynamics and her policy agenda.Beyond the historic firstsThe four contests illustrate the growing visibility of Indian-origin candidates in American politics. They also demonstrate that the community is not represented by a single political ideology: Ramaswamy is a Republican, while Raman, Sethi and Dandiya are Democrats.The offices they seek carry very different responsibilities. A governor leads a state executive branch; a mayor oversees city administration; a state legislator shapes laws and budgets; and a member of Congress votes on federal legislation.Historic firsts can broaden perceptions of who belongs in positions of power. But representation is only one part of the story. Voters will also judge these candidates on housing, education, healthcare, economic opportunity and public safety.November 3 could therefore become a significant date for Indian-American political representation. Whether it delivers the anticipated breakthroughs will depend on the choices voters make at the ballot box.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: After a chef was diagnosed with terminal cancer, his restaurant community created a charity; it has now provided $18 million in financial assistance to 40,000 food workers
articles.summary: Atlanta chef Ryan Hidinger received a terminal cancer diagnosis that threatened to derail his life and the restaurant he had hoped to open with his wife,
articles.body: Atlanta chef Ryan Hidinger received a terminal cancer diagnosis that threatened to derail his life and the restaurant he had hoped to open with his wife, Jen. What followed was an extraordinary response from friends, colleagues and the wider restaurant community, who rallied to help the couple through an incredibly difficult period. Their generosity eventually inspired Giving Kitchen, a nonprofit dedicated to supporting food service workers facing personal emergencies. More than a decade later, the organisation has provided $18 million in financial assistance and helped 40,000 workers across the United States.How a chef’s cancer diagnosis led to Giving Kitchen helping 40,000 food workersThe beginnings of Giving Kitchen were rooted in a personal crisis rather than a formal charitable initiative. As explained in the organisation’s official account of its history, Hidinger was working at Muss & Turner’s in the Atlanta area while preparing to launch Staplehouse, a restaurant he had envisioned with his wife.The diagnosis changed those plans dramatically. Hidinger had stage-four cancer, and the couple suddenly faced the financial and emotional pressures associated with treatment. His colleagues at Muss & Turner’s, including owners Ryan Turner, Todd Mussman and Chris Hall, stepped in to help.The restaurant community organised a fundraising event called Team Hidi in early 2013. According to The Bitter Southerner, approximately 800 restaurant workers and supporters attended the fundraiser, generating more than $275,000.The money was intended to help Hidinger and his wife cover expenses while he underwent treatment. However, the fundraiser raised far more than the couple initially needed, creating an opportunity to extend the generosity to other workers facing similar difficulties.From one family’s crisis to a wider missionThe idea for a nonprofit emerged during conversations among Hidinger, his wife and friends who had witnessed the community’s response. They realised that restaurant workers experiencing illness, injury or other emergencies often needed support beyond what their employers could provide.The organisation was founded in 2013, with the initial fundraising proceeds helping other food service workers in crisis. Its mission became providing emergency financial assistance and connecting workers with resources that could help them regain stability.The Local Palate reported how the organisation gradually developed beyond direct financial support. It established a stability network that connects workers with services relating to health, housing and family needs.Hidinger died following his cancer battle, but the charity continued to grow around the principles of compassion, gratitude and community that had shaped the response to his diagnosis. His wife, Jen Hidinger-Kendrick, remained closely involved in its development.What does Giving Kitchen provide to workers in crisisThe charity's current impact figures show how the original idea has developed into a nationwide support system. Giving Kitchen's impact report records $18 million in financial assistance awarded since its founding, alongside 40,000 food service workers helped across all 50 US states and Washington DC.The organisation's assistance is designed to address immediate financial pressures that can become overwhelming when a worker experiences an unexpected emergency. According to its impact figures, the charity has provided 7,930 months of rent, helping people remain in their homes while dealing with difficult circumstances.Its support has also helped more than 5,000 children of clients avoid hunger. The same report estimates that 73.5% of financial assistance recipients avoid homelessness, while $695,000 in late fees has been avoided through the assistance provided.The charity expanded beyond financial assistanceThe organisation recognised that some problems affecting hospitality workers required specialised support. Following Anthony Bourdain's death in 2018, Giving Kitchen introduced suicide prevention training through the QPR Institute. The training, based on question, persuasion and refer, helps participants recognise warning signs and respond when someone may be experiencing a mental health crisis.The Local Palate documented Giving Kitchen's efforts to address substance abuse and addiction within the food service industry. Its programme helps people undertake inpatient treatment by covering essential expenses such as housing, reducing the financial pressure on individuals and their families during recovery. Financial aid may keep a household afloat, while access to healthcare, counselling or other services can help address the circumstances behind the emergency.A restaurant community continues to support the missionGiving Kitchen also continues to celebrate its origins through Team Hidi, an annual event that brings together chefs, bartenders and other food industry professionals. Giving Kitchen received the James Beard Foundation's Humanitarian of the Year award in 2019, acknowledging its work supporting food service professionals.During the COVID-19 shutdowns, Giving Kitchen faced a surge in demand as hospitality workers lost jobs and businesses closed. The charity maintained its focus on emergency assistance while directing other workers towards resources such as unemployment support.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Republicans feeling blue as US midterms get under way: Key races, Indian-Americans in fray & states to watch
articles.summary: The battle for control of the US Congress is under way, and Republicans have reason to be nervous.
articles.body: The battle for control of the US Congress is under way, and Republicans have reason to be nervous.As millions of Americans head to polling stations on November 3, the latest surveys point to a difficult electoral environment for President Donald Trump's Republican Party, with Democrats building a substantial lead in the national congressional preference polls and gaining ground in several traditionally Republican states.The elections are shaping up as a referendum on Trump's second presidency, with voters weighing the administration's handling of the economy, the cost of living, immigration, tariffs and the war involving Iran.For Democrats, the midterms offer an opportunity to turn dissatisfaction with the White House into control of Congress. For Republicans, the challenge is to prevent a midterm backlash from becoming a decisive repudiation of Trump's political agenda.All 435 seats in the House of Representatives, 35 Senate seats and 36 governorships are being contested.The outcome will determine not only who controls the legislative agenda for the remaining two years of Trump's presidency but also how much political leverage the president retains heading into the 2028 presidential election.The numbersThe national polling picture has shifted considerably in the Democrats' favour in the final stretch of the campaign. A polling aggregation updated on November 3 puts the Democratic advantage on the generic congressional ballot at approximately 8.4 percentage points.The figures represent national preferences for congressional elections, rather than predictions of individual seat outcomes. Nevertheless, a Democratic lead of this magnitude is significant, particularly given how narrow the Republican majority in the House is.(function(){function e(){window.addEventListener(`message`,function(e){if(e.data[`datawrapper-height`]!==void 0){var t=document.querySelectorAll(`iframe`);for(var n in e.data[`datawrapper-height`])for(var r=0,i;i=t[r];r++)if(i.contentWindow===e.source){var a=e.data[`datawrapper-height`][n]+`px`;i.style.height=a}}})}e()})();An earlier RealClearPolling average, cited by Al Jazeera on October 31, had Democrats ahead 51.4% to 43.2%, an 8.2-point advantage. An Economist/YouGov survey also found that 44% of registered voters expected Democrats to control the House after the election, against 31% who expected Republicans to retain it.The Senate picture was less settled in that survey: 39% expected Democrats to win control, while 36% anticipated a Republican majority.Perhaps the most consequential development is the latest forecast from election analyst Nate Silver's Silver Bulletin. Its final November 3 forecast says a Democratic House majority now looks almost certain and that Democrats have also moved into a strong position to capture the Senate.The model's polling averages show Democrats ahead in practically every major Senate battleground, including Texas, Ohio, Michigan, Maine and Iowa. Even states that Republicans would ordinarily expect to defend comfortably have become competitive.The figures are especially striking in Texas, Ohio and Kansas, where Democrats are attempting to break through in states that have traditionally leaned Republican in federal elections.However, polls are not predictions. A lead of three or four percentage points can disappear within the margin of error, and turnout, undecided voters and differences between likely-voter and registered-voter samples could still change the outcome.Why the Democrats believe a blue wave is possibleHistorically, the party occupying the White House tends to lose ground in midterm elections. The president's party has lost House seats in 18 of the last 20 midterm elections over the past 80 years, making the November vote particularly uncomfortable for Trump.But this election is also being shaped by a combination of issues that Democrats believe have created an unusually difficult environment for Republicans.The economy and cost of living: Affordability has emerged as a central campaign issue. Voters are concerned about everyday expenses, energy prices, healthcare costs and the pressure on household budgets. Republicans are facing questions about whether Trump's economic policies have delivered the relief promised during the 2024 presidential campaign. Democrats have sought to connect tariffs and the Iran war to higher costs for consumers, farmers and businesses. In Iowa, for instance, the impact of tariffs and the rising cost of diesel and fertiliser have become central to the campaign. Rural voters, traditionally an important Republican constituency, are being targeted by Democrats with an affordability message.The Iran war: The war involving Iran has become another major political vulnerability for the administration. Republicans are facing criticism over its economic consequences, particularly energy prices and the wider uncertainty surrounding American military involvement. The issue has also created a difficult balancing act for GOP candidates who must defend the president's foreign policy while attempting to keep the focus on domestic concerns.Trump's approval ratings: Trump's popularity is another major concern for Republicans. The New York Times polling average put his approval rating at approximately 37% ahead of Election Day. Democrats have sought to turn dissatisfaction with the president into votes against Republican candidates, even in constituencies that Trump won comfortably in 2024.Early voting and turnout: More than 43 million Americans had already voted early, either in person or through returned mail ballots, five days before Election Day, according to an Associated Press analysis. That was nearly 10 million more than at the equivalent stage before the 2022 midterms. Texas had recorded more than 6.3 million early ballots by October 28, against 4.2 million at the corresponding stage in 2022 — an increase of around 50%. Georgia had also crossed 2.5 million early ballots by October 30, surpassing its 2022 early-voting figure of 2.3 million. The numbers indicate heightened electoral engagement, although early voting figures alone cannot establish which party will benefit.The House: Republicans' biggest vulnerabilityThe party entered the election with 219 seats against the Democrats' 214, with two vacancies. Democrats therefore need a net gain of just four seats to secure a majority.That relatively small hurdle has made dozens of districts competitive, including several that Trump carried in 2024.The challenge for Republicans is compounded by the fact that the president's party generally faces a midterm disadvantage. Democrats, meanwhile, have been encouraged by the national polling advantage and their performance in a number of special elections.The Cook Political Report and other election forecasters have identified a broad collection of Republican-held seats that could become vulnerable.Among the most important House contests are:NEW YORK Republican Congressman Mike Lawler faces Democrat Cait Conley in New York's 17th Congressional District. The constituency is particularly important because it is among the few Republican-held districts that Kamala Harris carried in the 2024 presidential election. Lawler has built his political identity around appealing to moderate voters, but the national political environment could make his re-election considerably more difficult. Conley is attempting to capitalise on dissatisfaction with Trump and turn the district's Democratic lean in the presidential election into a congressional victory. The latest polling aggregation puts Conley approximately two percentage points ahead, making this one of the most closely watched Republican-held seats.IOWA Iowa's first congressional district is another important test of whether Democrats can win back voters in traditionally Republican territory. Republican Congresswoman Mariannette Miller-Meeks faces Democrat Christina Bohannan, who has unsuccessfully challenged her in previous elections. The contest has become more competitive amid concerns about tariffs, farm costs and the wider economic outlook. Democrats have also invested heavily in the district. Reuters reported that they had spent approximately $11 million compared with $7 million by Republicans. The latest polling aggregation showed Bohannan with a substantial lead, although the district's Republican lean and the history of Miller-Meeks' victories make this a race worth watching closely.TEXAS Texas has become a particularly important battleground because of the Republican effort to redraw congressional boundaries to improve the party's chances of retaining its House majority. Republicans hoped the redistricting exercise would create additional favourable seats. But Democrats are attempting to turn the backlash against the process into an electoral advantage. Several Texas districts are now being closely monitored, including the 9th District, where the polling aggregation shows Democrat Alex Mealer narrowly ahead of the Republican incumbent. The 15th District is another contest to watch, with Republican Monica De La Cruz facing a challenge from Democrat Bobby Pulido. The outcome will help establish whether Republican efforts to reshape congressional boundaries have delivered the expected advantage.Other House races to watchArizona's 1st District: Democrat Amish Shah is challenging Republican Jay Feely in a competitive open-seat contest. Shah's campaign has attracted significant outside spending, and the latest polling aggregation gives him a four-point advantage.Florida's 22nd District: Democrat Pia Dandiya is challenging Republican Casey Askar in a seat that has been rated a toss-up by major election forecasters.Pennsylvania's 7th District: Republican Ryan Mackenzie faces Democrat Ryan Crosswell in another closely watched contest.Michigan's 10th District: Democrat Christina Hines and Republican Michael Bouchard are competing for an open seat after John James entered the gubernatorial race.Montana's 1st District: Democrat Sam Forstag is attempting to unseat Republican Aaron Flint in a district Trump won comfortably in 2024.New Jersey's 7th District: Democrat Rebecca Bennett is challenging Republican Tom Kean Jr., who has faced criticism over his absence from congressional votes.These contests are part of a much larger battle. CBS News identified 42 House races that could determine which party controls the chamber.Senate: Could Democrats pull off an even bigger upset?The Senate battle is more complicated.Republicans currently hold 53 seats against the Democrats' 47. Democrats need a net gain of four seats to reach a majority, assuming the existing chamber alignment.This is a considerably more difficult proposition than winning the House because Republicans are defending seats in a number of states Trump carried by comfortable margins in 2024. But the latest surveys have given Democrats fresh hope.Five Senate contests deserve particular attention.1. Texas: James Talarico's opportunity to make historyTexas is emerging as one of the biggest potential Democratic breakthroughs of the election.Democrat James Talarico is challenging Republican Ken Paxton, the state's attorney general, for a Senate seat.Paxton defeated incumbent Republican Senator John Cornyn in the GOP primary, but his nomination has raised questions about whether Republicans have selected the strongest possible candidate for a general election contest.His history of personal and political controversies has given Democrats an opening.Talarico, a state representative and former teacher, has sought to build a campaign around economic issues, healthcare and a broader appeal to voters dissatisfied with the political establishment.The November 1 New York Times/Siena poll put Talarico ahead 50% to 43%.A polling average also showed him leading by approximately three points. A Democratic victory would be particularly significant: the party has not won a Texas Senate election since 1988.2. Michigan: Abdul El-Sayed takes on Mike RogersMichigan is another state where Democrats are hoping to make a significant gain.Democrat Abdul El-Sayed is challenging Republican Mike Rogers for an open Senate seat following the retirement of Senator Gary Peters.El-Sayed, a progressive former Michigan health official, won a divisive Democratic primary against a more moderate opponent.Rogers, a former congressman, is attempting to return to the Senate after losing his previous election battle against Elissa Slotkin.The latest New York Times/Siena survey gave El-Sayed a commanding 53%-42% lead.This is particularly important because Michigan is a major battleground state where the Democratic candidate's performance could help establish whether the party's national polling advantage is translating into votes.3. Ohio: Sherrod Brown attempts a comebackFormer Democratic Senator Sherrod Brown is attempting to reclaim his seat after losing his re-election bid in 2024.He faces Republican Senator Jon Husted, who was appointed to the seat vacated by JD Vance after Vance became vice-president.Brown has sought to position himself as a champion of working-class voters, an important constituency in a state that has moved increasingly towards Republicans in recent elections.His campaign is attempting to make the election about manufacturing jobs, economic insecurity and the cost of living.The New York Times/Siena poll put Brown ahead 49%-44%, suggesting that Ohio could become one of the biggest Democratic surprises of the night.4. Maine: Susan Collins faces a serious challengeRepublican Senator Susan Collins is fighting to retain her seat against Democrat Troy Jackson.Collins has survived several difficult election campaigns and has often benefited from her ability to attract support beyond the Republican base.But the political environment is different this time. Maine voted for Kamala Harris in 2024, and Democrats believe the state's electorate could turn against Republicans in the midterms.The November 1 Siena poll showed Jackson leading Collins 51%-45%.A Democratic victory here would be particularly consequential because Collins has been a prominent Republican figure in the Senate for decades.5. Alaska: Mary Peltola threatens another Republican seatFormer Democratic Congresswoman Mary Peltola is challenging Republican Senator Dan Sullivan in Alaska.Alaska is not an obvious Democratic pickup opportunity. The state has a strong Republican voting history and has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 2008.But Peltola has demonstrated an ability to appeal to voters beyond the traditional Democratic base.The latest Siena poll showed her leading Sullivan 48%-46%.Even a narrow victory would be a major breakthrough for Democrats and could prove decisive in the battle for Senate control.Other Senate contests that could decide controlStateDemocratic candidateRepublican candidateLatest polling pictureKansasAdam HamiltonRoger MarshallHamilton +5IowaJosh TurekAshley HinsonTurek +1GeorgiaJon OssoffMike CollinsOssoff +9.2North CarolinaRoy CooperMichael WhatleyCooper +10.9New HampshireChris PappasJohn SununuPappas +7.3NebraskaIndependent/Democratic-aligned candidatePete RickettsRicketts +0.9Kansas is especially interesting. Democrat Adam Hamilton is attempting to become the first Democrat to win a Senate election in the state since 1932.The race against Republican Senator Roger Marshall has become competitive because of concerns over affordability, energy costs and the Iran war.Georgia, meanwhile, is a test of whether Republicans can unseat Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff. Republican Mike Collins is challenging him, but the latest polling averages suggest Ossoff has a substantial advantage.North Carolina is another important opportunity for Democrats. Former governor Roy Cooper is running against Republican Michael Whatley in an open-seat contest. Cooper's popularity and statewide political experience have made him a formidable challenger.Together, these races could determine whether Democrats can overcome the unfavourable Senate map and take control of the chamber.Governor races: Democrats eye a historic breakthroughWhile congressional control is the biggest national prize, the gubernatorial contests could produce a political realignment of their own.A total of 36 states are electing governors, representing approximately 80% of the US population. Nineteen of those contests involve open seats.Democrats are hoping to win control of a majority of governors' offices for the first time in two decades. Their last such breakthrough came in 2006, when they flipped six governorships during the midterm elections of George W Bush's presidency.The most closely watched races include:1. Ohio: Vivek Ramaswamy vs Amy ActonThis is arguably the most closely watched gubernatorial contest from an Indian-American perspective.Republican Vivek Ramaswamy, backed by Trump, is running against Democrat Amy Acton, the former Ohio health director.Ramaswamy entered the campaign with considerable national visibility, having previously contested the 2024 Republican presidential nomination and later worked with the Trump administration's Department of Government Efficiency initiative.Acton, meanwhile, is seeking to make the race a referendum on Republican leadership in the state.The latest New York Times/Siena survey put Acton ahead 49%-43%. Another November 1 survey by Survey 160 showed her leading 51%-44%.The polling average on November 2 gave Acton a lead of approximately 3.8 points.The campaign has also been marred by controversy over a political advertisement involving Acton's family, which attracted criticism from both Democrats and some prominent Republicans.A Democratic victory would be a significant setback for Trump, who has publicly backed Ramaswamy.2. Texas: Gina Hinojosa vs Greg AbbottDemocrat Gina Hinojosa is mounting a challenge to Republican Governor Greg Abbott, who is seeking another term.No Democrat has won a statewide election in Texas since 1994, making the contest particularly significant.Hinojosa has sought to make affordability, healthcare and economic opportunity central to her campaign.The New York Times/Siena survey showed her narrowly ahead 48%-47%, putting Abbott under unusual pressure in a state where Republicans have dominated statewide politics for decades.3. Georgia: An opening for DemocratsGeorgia has not elected a Democratic governor since 1998.The open-seat contest has therefore attracted considerable national attention, with Democrats believing that the wider political climate could help them overcome the state's Republican lean.4. Iowa and Alaska: Testing Republican strongholdsBoth states have competitive open-seat gubernatorial contests.In Iowa, Democrat Rob Sand is challenging Republican Zach Lahn, while in Alaska Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins is facing Republican Bernadette Wilson.The Siena survey gave the Democratic candidates leads of 51%-43% and 54%-46%, respectively.5. Florida: Can Democrats make another breakthrough?Republican Byron Donalds, a prominent Trump ally, is challenging Democrat David Jolly.Florida has become increasingly Republican in recent elections, but Democrats believe the economic environment could make the contest more competitive than expected.Indian-Americans in the fray: A growing political footprintThe 2026 elections are also important for the Indian-American community, with candidates of Indian origin contesting positions ranging from the US House of Representatives to governorships, attorney-general offices and local government.Read also | Indian-American candidates in 2026 US midterms: Key races, profiles, latest polling & what's at stakeThe growing presence of Indian-Americans in American politics reflects a broader shift in the country's political landscape. Their participation is no longer confined to a handful of congressional constituencies. Candidates are competing in states across the country, representing both major political parties.Among the prominent candidates are Democratic lawmakers Ro Khanna, Pramila Jayapal, Ami Bera and Suhas Subramanyam, all seeking another term in Congress.Republican Vivek Ramaswamy is the most high-profile Indian-origin candidate contesting a gubernatorial election.Other Indian-origin candidates to watchThe election also features several Indian-American candidates seeking to expand their political representation beyond the traditional congressional contests.Amish Shah — Arizona: The Democrat and former Arizona state legislator is challenging Republican Jay Feely in the 1st Congressional District. The race has attracted significant outside spending and could become an important Democratic pickup.Pia Dandiya — Florida: Dandiya is contesting Florida's 22nd Congressional District against Republican Casey Askar. The race has been rated a toss-up by several election forecasters.Saritha Komatireddy — New York: The Republican candidate is challenging Democratic Attorney General Letitia James. A former federal prosecutor, Komatireddy has worked on national security and organised-crime cases. Polls have shown James with a lead.Nithya Raman — Los Angeles: The Indian-origin Los Angeles City Council member is challenging incumbent Mayor Karen Bass. They could determine the political trajectory of Trump's remaining two years in office.A Democratic takeover of the House would give the opposition control over committees, investigations, legislative priorities and congressional oversight.It could also complicate the administration's ability to pass major legislation, particularly on immigration, taxation, federal spending and foreign policy.A Democratic Senate majority would have even greater consequences. articles.title: Taylor Swift donated proceeds from her 'Wildest Dreams' music video to African conservation; the organisation now manages 22 protected areas across 12 countries
articles.summary: Taylor Swift’s 2015 music video for ‘Wildest Dreams’ attracted attention for its sweeping African landscapes, but the release also brought criticism over
articles.body: Taylor Swift’s 2015 music video for ‘Wildest Dreams’ attracted attention for its sweeping African landscapes, but the release also brought criticism over how the continent was represented. Set against scenes of wildlife and open countryside, the video prompted questions about its colonial-era imagery and the absence of African characters. Away from the debate, Swift had attached a charitable commitment to the project, directing its proceeds towards African conservation. The beneficiary, African Parks, has since expanded its work across the continent and now manages protected areas in several countries, supporting landscapes that are home to some of Africa’s most threatened wildlife.Taylor Swift donated ‘Wildest Dreams’ music video proceeds to African Parks‘Wildest Dreams’ arrived on 30 August 2015, during the MTV Video Music Awards weekend. Directed by Joseph Kahn, the production presented Swift as a Hollywood actress working on a film in Africa during the 1950s. Actor Scott Eastwood played her romantic co-star. Giraffes, zebras and lions appeared throughout the footage, alongside wide shots of savannah landscapes and other scenery.The charitable arrangement was made clear at the end of the video. Swift pledged all proceeds generated by the production to wild animal conservation through the African Parks Foundation of America. The organisation acknowledged the contribution in September 2015, confirming that the singer was donating the video's proceeds to support its conservation work.The announcement concerned the music video, rather than a commitment to donate royalties from the entire ‘1989’ album or the ‘Wildest Dreams’ single.Music video faces criticism over its portrayal of AfricaThe donation was announced alongside a production that attracted criticism for its visual treatment of the continent. Although filmed in African locations, the video centred on a romance between two white Hollywood performers, with wildlife and scenery providing much of the setting. Its period styling, reminiscent of mid-20th-century adventure films, led commentators to question the image of Africa being presented to an international audience.Some critics argued that the production relied on a colonial-era safari aesthetic, giving the continent the appearance of an exotic backdrop while leaving African people largely outside the story. The discussion extended beyond the casting to the wider issue of how Western entertainment has historically depicted African landscapes and communities.Kahn responded publicly to the criticism, explaining that the story was intended to depict a fictional film production set in the 1950s rather than make a statement about colonialism. He also pointed to the involvement of Black professionals in the production, including producer Jil Hardin. His response did not end the wider discussion about representation, but it clarified the creative premise behind the video.African Parks has grown into a major conservation networkAfrican Parks was established in 2000 in response to the deterioration of protected areas across Africa. Poor management, inadequate funding and declining wildlife populations had left many national parks struggling to maintain their ecological value.The organisation developed a model in which it enters long-term agreements with national governments to take responsibility for managing protected areas. Governments retain ownership of the land and authority over national policy, while African Parks oversees day-to-day operations, conservation programmes, staffing and financial management.Its work has grown considerably since its first management agreement in Malawi in 2003. According to its latest organisational information, African Parks now manages 24 national parks and protected areas across 13 countries, covering more than 20 million hectares. These include landscapes in Angola, Benin, Chad, Ethiopia, Malawi, Mozambique, Rwanda, Zambia and Zimbabwe, among others.The figure of 22 protected areas across 12 countries appeared in the organisation's 2023 annual report and in some of its earlier published material. Its current figures reflect further expansion. Its stated ambition is to manage 30 parks by 2030.Conservation work extends beyond protecting wildlifeAfrican Parks' responsibilities involve more than keeping animals within protected boundaries. Its teams work on restoring damaged ecosystems, monitoring wildlife populations, tackling illegal hunting and improving the conditions needed for threatened species to survive.Rangers carry out patrols and help prevent poaching and other illegal activities. Conservation programmes can also involve moving animals between protected areas, reintroducing species that have disappeared from particular landscapes and managing populations where wildlife numbers have changed significantly. Scientific monitoring helps determine whether these interventions are working.The organisation also places community development within its conservation model. Its approach recognises that people living around protected areas have a direct relationship with the land and its resources. Education, employment, local businesses and opportunities to participate in park-related decisions form part of its work. Tourism and other sustainable commercial activities can generate revenue that is reinvested in park management.Malawi's Majete reserve illustrates the scale of restorationOne of African Parks' earlier projects was Majete Wildlife Reserve in Malawi, where it signed a 25-year management agreement with the government in 2003. The reserve had experienced years of wildlife decline, weak protection and limited tourism before the partnership began.The rehabilitation programme included strengthening ranger operations and restoring wildlife populations through carefully planned reintroductions. Black rhinos and buffalo were brought back in 2003, followed by elephants in 2006, leopards in 2011 and lions in 2012. Giraffes and cheetahs were introduced in later years.African Parks' 2019 annual report supports this figure. Its newer Majete page says more than 3,000 animals representing 17 species. The reserve also developed livelihood initiatives, including a beekeeping programme involving hundreds of local participants.Local communities remain part of the organisation's approachThe scale of African Parks' operations also depends on the people working in and around its protected areas. Its published figures record more than 5,000 employees across its operating countries, with 97% of staff being nationals of the countries where they work.These roles extend beyond ranger patrols to include ecological research, administration, infrastructure, tourism, community development and park operations. The organisation works with national authorities and local communities, with the intention of making protected areas viable over the long term rather than relying solely on external conservation funding.Swift's 2015 contribution was one public example of celebrity support for this work. African Parks has since expanded its management portfolio, although its published material does not establish that the singer's donation directly financed any particular park or restoration project.You use AI every day. articles.body: Iran and the United States remain far from reaching a deal to end their war, a senior Iranian official told Reuters on Tuesday, warning that Tehran would not accept Washington's "excessive demands" and that its conditions must be met for the Strait of Hormuz to reopen.According to the Reuters report, the remarks came amid intensified diplomatic efforts to prevent a fresh escalation of the conflict, with Qatari mediators travelling to Tehran on Monday night to discuss a draft US-Iran agreement that has been under negotiation for the past eight days.The Iranian official said mediators were working to bridge differences between Washington and Tehran, but warned that nuclear negotiations could begin only after Iran's conditions were fulfilled."Mediators are working hard to narrow gaps between Tehran and Washington," the senior Iranian official said, adding, "Tehran's conditions must be met if the US wants Hormuz reopened."The official also said Tehran would not accept Washington's "excessive demands" and warned that Iran would respond forcefully, within the region and beyond, to any fresh US strikes.Meanwhile, the United States carried out what it described as "defensive" strikes on Iran's Qeshm Island overnight, targeting surface-to-air missile systems allegedly used against American assets, according to a US official. Another US official said the strikes appeared limited and did not signal a resumption of major combat operations.In response, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) claimed that it had shot down a US MQ-9 drone and two Lucas drones near the Strait of Hormuz.Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf said the responsibility for preventing further escalation now rested with Washington, following what he described as Tehran's "strong and rational response".Qatar's foreign ministry spokesperson Majed al-Ansari said on Tuesday that both the United States and Iran remained committed to mediation and were reviewing proposals put forward by intermediaries. articles.title: A Missouri woman rescued an orphaned fawn after its mother was killed; 13 years later, the deer had her own babies and brought them back to the family’s garden
articles.summary: Orphaned fawn rescue in Missouri rarely leads to a bond as lasting as the one between Lorrie Brown and her pet deer, Buttons.
articles.body: Orphaned fawn rescue in Missouri rarely leads to a bond as lasting as the one between Lorrie Brown and her pet deer, Buttons. Taken in after her mother was killed, the doe lived with Brown’s family in southwest Missouri for more than thirteen and a half years, growing up beside two children, a golden retriever and a cat. Brown, now 57, describes her as a genuine member of the household, and Buttons repeatedly brought her fawns to the people who had raised her. Brown even wrote a children’s book about the close friendship between Buttons and the family’s dog, GBro.A roadside death, a phone call and a Missouri woman who offered an orphaned fawn a new homeFifteen years ago, Brown received a call about a mother deer that had been hit by a vehicle near the caller’s home. Her baby was left standing in the caller’s yard. Because the family lived close to the roadside, they were searching for somewhere the fawn could grow up safely, far from traffic.Brown told People she figured her home, which sits on a sizeable stretch of land, would be the ideal place to relocate the animal. Her family named the fawn Buttons.How a social, trusting doe formed a legendary trio with GBro the dog and Rabbit the catButtons eventually formed a “legendary trio” with GBro and the family’s cat, Rabbit, who lived to the age of twenty-two. Brown said she was surprised by how much the doe trusted the dog.Deer, she explained, are such social animals that they “literally have the fear of missing out”. Buttons proved the point whenever Brown’s daughter had swimming lessons. The doe would appear in the backyard the moment she heard them, expecting the children to pet and fuss over her.How trail walks with a deer, cats and dogs on a property won over a devoted online audienceSix years ago, Brown began documenting life with Buttons. In 2020, she was sharing posts on Facebook, and followers kept telling her the clips brought them joy. Her son, who was twenty-one at the time, encouraged her to try TikTok. She admits she had no idea what it was, but reasoned that if he was happy for her to post, she could not be that uncool.Around then, Brown and her husband were building a hiking trail system on their land, which now stretches to almost fourteen miles. Buttons accompanied her on the routes, and cats and dogs often tagged along too. Brown said she receives comments every day from people who describe the walks as a break from politics, stress and a troubled world. She now shares her animals under the username @brownhikingtrails.Two deaths within two months: the heartbreak of losing Buttons and Biscuit during the rutAbout four years ago, the family found another baby deer on their trails, covered in maggots. They were unsure she would survive, but they rescued her and named her Biscuit. She lived for nineteen months before a car struck her.Buttons was also struck and killed within two months of Biscuit. Roads are scarce near the family’s home, but both deaths happened during the rut, the mating season when bucks chase does. “Our hearts were so broken,” Brown recalled, adding that followers felt the loss just as deeply because they had grown so attached to the deer and the family’s dogs.How an orphaned fawn named Benny and his duck friend Pip helped heal a heartbroken familyA year after the double loss, a follower who had found Brown’s page called about a fawn whose mother had been killed by coyotes. Benny arrived last summer and, in Brown’s words, “healed everybody’s hearts”. He lived in her garden, sleeping near her ducks and spending his days beside them, and became best friends with one called Pip.Benny now roams freely on the family’s land, yet he is there every morning and evening and still hikes with them daily. He is old enough for his first rut and to find “little girlfriends”, as Brown puts it. Because he is the first buck she has raised, she cannot be certain the routine will last. She compares her worry to the feeling of watching her own children leave for college, and says she feels at peace whenever she sees him lying in the yard. Giving young animals freedom while hoping they stay safe, she said, is the hardest part. She does not expect to meet his fawns, since bucks typically have little to do with their young after birth. Benny’s friendship with the ducks is the subject of another of her books, Benny and the Ducks.Buttons had eleven pregnancies, and now seventeen or eighteen deer visit the yard each morningButtons gave birth eleven times while she lived with the family. Each time, Brown walked up to her as soon as the fawn arrived, finding the doe licking her newborn clean and willing to let the family hold it. Buttons would also leave her fawns with GBro while she went about her day.That line of descendants now fills the property. Brown estimates that seventeen or eighteen deer gather in the yard each morning, and she believes nearly every one is related to Buttons, because her young went on to have young of their own. Benny is the first deer there with no family link to her, so the two bloodlines will eventually mix.Brown feeds the deer to tempt them back, and says she does it because they are all connected to Buttons and she sees it as looking after her legacy. In her experience, deer have no family of their own until they make one. Benny had the ducks and the household, and Buttons had the family, the dog and the cat, until each began building a family and bringing it to Brown’s door.Brown’s family, including her new grandson, shares her love for the animals. Most mornings she carries the boy outside, where he pets Benny and watches the ducks and deer. Followers tell her they love seeing a grandchild grow up in the same animal-filled surroundings her own children did, Brown told the source, and she says his face lights up whenever he sees Benny.You use AI every day. articles.title: A chimpanzee spent almost his entire 32-year life inside an Indiana garage; after his owner died, rescuers launched an urgent mission to save him
articles.summary: A 32-year-old chimpanzee named Toby spent almost his entire life confined to the garage of a rural home in Indiana, with little opportunity to experience
articles.body: A 32-year-old chimpanzee named Toby spent almost his entire life confined to the garage of a rural home in Indiana, with little opportunity to experience the world beyond his enclosure. His situation became urgent after his owner died, reportedly leaving instructions for the animal to be shot rather than transferred to another home. With the owner's family allegedly intending to follow those wishes, animal welfare advocates and federal officials had only a short window to intervene. Their efforts eventually helped Toby escape a lifetime of isolation and begin a new chapter at a Florida sanctuary.The 32-year-old chimpanzee rescued from an Indiana garageAccording to the Animal Legal Defense Fund (ALDF), the rescue effort began on a Friday afternoon just before a long holiday weekend. Brittany Peet, the organisation's director of Transparency and Regulatory Affairs, received an alarming call about Toby from a contact who had heard about the situation through a concerned member of the public.The information was particularly disturbing. Toby's owner had recently died and had reportedly left instructions that the chimpanzee should be killed after his death. The owner's family was said to be considering carrying out those wishes, putting Toby's life at immediate risk.Peet, an attorney specialising in protecting captive wild animals, understood that there was little time to waste. She knew that chimpanzees are protected under the federal Endangered Species Act, which prohibits killing members of protected species without the required permit. In Toby's circumstances, such permission would not have been granted.She immediately prepared an official complaint and sent it to a senior official at the US Fish and Wildlife Service, the federal agency responsible for enforcing the law.But waiting for the complaint to be processed could have left Toby in danger over the holiday weekend. Peet therefore contacted another person who worked closely with the agency on wildlife trafficking issues. Although both contacts were already travelling for their holiday plans, they stopped to help.Federal officials stepped in before it was too lateThe urgency of the situation prompted an Indiana-based Fish and Wildlife Service agent to travel to the property within hours of receiving the complaint.The agent informed the people responsible for Toby that killing him would constitute a federal crime. The intervention also secured assurances that the chimpanzee would not be harmed.This immediate response prevented a potentially tragic outcome, but rescuing Toby was only the first part of the challenge. After spending more than three decades in a private home, he needed somewhere suitable to live, with people experienced in caring for chimpanzees that had been kept as pets.Peet contacted the Center for Great Apes in Florida, a sanctuary accredited by the Global Federation of Animal Sanctuaries. The organisation had experience rehabilitating chimpanzees rescued from private homes and the pet trade, making it a suitable place for Toby.The sanctuary agreed to take him in. The ALDF, with financial support from its supporters, arranged and funded his transport from Indiana to Florida. Expert veterinarians also travelled with Toby to monitor his health and ensure his safety throughout the journey.What was life like for Toby before his rescueToby's difficult circumstances began when he was very young. He was born at a roadside zoo in Oklahoma and taken away from his mother while still an infant so that he could be sold as a pet.This is a common practice in the wild animal pet trade, where young primates are separated from their mothers much earlier than they naturally would be. In the wild, chimpanzees remain closely connected to their mothers for years and grow up within complex family groups.Toby was denied that experience. For almost his entire life, he had little or no opportunity to interact with other chimpanzees. The ALDF describes this prolonged social isolation as one of the most serious forms of psychological suffering a primate can experience.His living conditions also prevented him from behaving naturally. Chimpanzees are active animals that climb, swing and travel considerable distances in search of food and other resources. Toby, however, spent more than 30 years inside a garage in rural Indiana.The organisation also reported that he appeared to have received little or no veterinary care during that period. Several sanctuaries and accredited zoos had previously offered to provide him with better living conditions, but his former owner never accepted those offers.His diet was another concern. Before arriving at the sanctuary, Toby had reportedly been fed mainly pizza, burritos and Mountain Dew. His new caregivers began introducing him to a more suitable diet designed around the nutritional needs of chimpanzees.Toby began discovering a different kind of life at the sanctuaryThe change in Toby's surroundings was significant. The Center for Great Apes reported that he was settling into his new home, showing curiosity and playfulness while gradually becoming comfortable with his caregivers.He was introduced to toys, enrichment activities and soft blankets. More importantly, he was given opportunities to make decisions for himself, including how he wanted to spend his time.One of his first independent choices involved where to sleep. On a warm night in Florida, Toby gathered his new blankets and made a nest outside. When it rained the following evening, he collected the blankets and moved them indoors.These small decisions represented a major change for an animal whose life had largely been controlled by humans.Toby was initially kept in a temporary enclosure while completing a quarantine period. This is a standard safety measure for new arrivals at the sanctuary, helping protect the health of other primates already living there.Even during this period, he was able to see and hear other chimpanzees. Caretakers noticed him quietly watching a chimpanzee housed nearby and listening closely to the calls of orangutans elsewhere on the sanctuary grounds.Once his quarantine was completed, the plan was to gradually introduce him to other chimpanzees. There was also the possibility that he could meet some of his siblings already living at the sanctuary.The ALDF noted that Toby's father, Joe, had also lived at the Center for Great Apes before his death the previous year. Joe had been captured in the wild and transferred between several facilities during his life before eventually finding sanctuary.Toby's rescue highlights the wider problem of keeping primates as petsThe ALDF believes Toby's story reflects a much larger problem involving the private ownership of chimpanzees and other primates.The organisation points to the case of Travis, another chimpanzee raised in a private home. As he grew older and stronger, his natural behaviour became increasingly difficult for his human family to manage. He eventually attacked a friend of his owner, was stabbed by the woman who had raised him and was fatally shot by a police officer.According to the ALDF, Toby may be among the last chimpanzees living in a private home in the US, but thousands of other primates are still believed to be kept as pets in unsuitable conditions.The organisation also highlighted a report finding that more than 1,600 primates were advertised for sale across just 4 social media platforms during a six-week period in 2025.To address the problem, the ALDF supports the proposed Captive Primate Safety Act, which would prohibit private ownership of apes and monkeys across the US. The proposed legislation would also restrict interstate and international trade in these animals for the pet market.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: In 2012, a US student was forgotten in a DEA cell for five days without food or water; he drank his own urine to survive, and the government later paid him $4.1 million in a settlement
articles.summary: A 23-year-old university student in the US was left inside a windowless Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) holding cell for nearly five days after
articles.body: A 23-year-old university student in the US was left inside a windowless Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) holding cell for nearly five days after agents decided he would not be charged in a drug investigation. With no food, drinking water or access to a toilet, he was forced to drink his own urine in a desperate attempt to stay alive. As his condition deteriorated, he screamed for help, tried to attract attention and eventually carved the words “Sorry Mom” into his arm. When agents finally discovered him, he was severely dehydrated and required hospital treatment. The incident, which took place in San Diego in April 2012, later led to a $4.1 million settlement with the US government and an investigation that exposed serious failures within the DEA's detention procedures.How Daniel Chong ended up in DEA custodyDaniel Chong, an engineering student at the University of California, San Diego, was at a friend's house in San Diego on April 21, 2012, when DEA agents carried out a drug raid. Investigators discovered approximately 18,000 ecstasy pills, along with other drugs and weapons, at the property.Chong was among nine people detained during the operation. He was questioned by agents and, according to his account, was told that he would not be charged and could go home. However, instead of being released, he was taken back to a small holding cell measuring approximately five feet by 10 feet.The cell had no windows, and Chong was left handcuffed with his hands behind his back. He was not provided with food or drinking water, and there were no toilet facilities. What was supposed to be a temporary detention turned into an ordeal lasting almost five days.He drank his own urine and carved 'Sorry Mom' into his armAs the hours passed, Chong became increasingly desperate. With no access to water, he resorted to drinking his own urine to prevent himself from dying of thirst. He also ingested methamphetamine that he found inside the cell, according to reports about the incident.He repeatedly screamed and tried to make noise to alert people outside. At one point, he attempted to reach a sprinkler system in the hope of getting water. He also broke his glasses and used a piece of them to carve the words “Sorry Mom” into his arm.His physical and psychological condition continued to deteriorate. Reports following the incident described severe dehydration, kidney damage, muscle degeneration, hallucinations and post-traumatic stress disorder. He was eventually discovered on April 25, 2012, in serious medical distress and taken to hospital, where he remained until April 29.Four DEA employees encountered him but failed to secure his releaseAn investigation by the Department of Justice's Office of the Inspector General examined how Chong could have remained inside the facility for so long without anyone ensuring his release.The investigation found that four DEA employees, including three case agents and a supervisor, had seen or heard Chong during the period of his detention. However, they assumed that someone else would return to process him. No one took responsibility for confirming that he had been released.The inspector general's findings also highlighted serious weaknesses in the facility's procedures. These included inadequate systems for tracking detainees, a lack of cameras inside individual holding cells, unreliable entry records and failures to conduct required daily checks.The report concluded that the detention resulted from a combination of employee misconduct and institutional failures. The agents had decided that Chong would not be charged, yet the procedures in place failed to ensure that he was actually released.Why the US government paid him $4.1 millionFollowing the incident, Chong's attorney, Eugene Iredale, filed a $20 million administrative claim against the federal government in May 2012. The claim sought compensation for the physical injuries and psychological trauma caused by the detention.In July 2013, the US government agreed to pay Chong $4.1 million to settle the claim. The payment was negotiated before a trial and was not a court-ordered award. The settlement brought the legal claim to an end without a court determining the government's liability through a verdict.The exact calculation behind the $4.1 million figure was not publicly itemised. However, the claim was based on the severity of Chong's ordeal, the medical consequences and the psychological harm he suffered. His attorney also said at the time that legal fees were capped at 20 per cent and estimated that Chong would receive at least $3.2 million after those fees.DEA apologised and changed its detention proceduresThe incident prompted the DEA to review its procedures for handling people held at its facilities. The agency apologised to Chong and introduced changes that included installing cameras in holding cells and requiring daily inspections of detainees.The case also led to disciplinary action against employees involved in the incident. In 2015, the DEA's Board of Professional Conduct issued reprimands and short suspensions to some of the personnel. The penalties included a seven-day suspension for the supervisor.The disciplinary measures drew criticism from officials and lawmakers who considered them too lenient given the seriousness of what had happened.You use AI every day. articles.title: Who were flying on doomed Learjet plane? Tech tycoon Adam Robinson, wife, children, nanny, family friends traveling to Bahamas on private jet
articles.summary: A family of four, including two young children, was among nine people killed after a private Learjet crashed in a residential neighbourhood in Florida on
articles.body: A family of four, including two young children, was among nine people killed after a private Learjet crashed in a residential neighbourhood in Florida on Sunday, November 1.The aircraft, a Learjet 60, was travelling from Austin, Texas, to the Bahamas when it plunged towards the ground and exploded into a fireball near Greenacres in Palm Beach County at around 12.50 pm local time.All nine people on board, including two pilots and seven passengers, died in the crash. One person on the ground sustained a leg injury, officials said.The families of seven passengers identified their loved ones in a joint statement on social media on Monday. The victims were identified as Adam Robinson, his wife Helen Sharp, their children Emma and Charlie, Rachael Reed, Charmi Fehr and Anita Maria Cetina.The children, Emma, 4, and Charlie, 2, were travelling with their parents. Anita Maria Cetina, who worked as their nanny, and family friends Rachael Reed and Charmi Fehr were also among the passengers.In the statement, the families described Adam and Helen as devoted parents and said their children were the centre of their lives. They also remembered Reed and Fehr as adventurous and full of joy, while describing Cetina as someone who had become an integral part of the family.The crash also claimed the lives of both pilots. The co-pilot was identified as 20-year-old Nathalia Filgueiras, whose mother confirmed her death. Filgueiras had earned her private pilot's licence at the age of 17 and had logged more than 1,300 flight hours, according to her mother.It remains unclear whether she was at the controls when the aircraft crashed.What happened before the crash?According to the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB), the aircraft was flying at approximately 35,000 feet when the pilots reported icing and moderate turbulence.The crew requested permission to climb to 37,000 feet to avoid precipitation. However, less than a minute later, the aircraft began descending rapidly and the pilots declared an emergency.Air traffic control recordings captured a crew member reporting that the aircraft was descending at 10,000 feet per minute, before the rate increased to 20,000 feet per minute.In the final moments, a crew member was heard saying, "We're going to crash into the ground." Flight-tracking data from Flightradar24 indicated that the descent rate at one point exceeded 32,000 feet per minute.What investigators have foundThe NTSB is investigating the crash, with weather conditions emerging as a major focus.NTSB investigators said there was evidence that parts of the aircraft may have broken off before it struck the ground. Officials warned that debris could be scattered some distance from the main impact site.Investigators are also trying to establish whether the aircraft's cockpit voice recorder was on board at the time of the accident. Maintenance records indicated that one had been installed.The impact created a massive crater near the entrance to a mobile home community. Around 600 residents were evacuated from the neighbourhood as emergency crews and investigators worked at the scene.Authorities urged residents not to move any aircraft debris they might find and instead report it to investigators.Who were Adam Robison and Helen?Robinson was an entrepreneur who founded the tech company Retention and regularly gave interviews about building a successful start-up. According to an online profile, Robinson previously worked on Wall Street for 10 years before launching an AI startup named GetEmail.Helen ran a communications firm called Influential PR. She also owned a successful, Aspen-based pottery studio called Helen Sharp Ceramics.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Trump unveiled the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool's latest repairs on November 2 after the blue coating failed and algae spread; a project once estimated below $2 million has drawn over $14 million in contracts
articles.summary: Donald Trump unveiled the completed repairs to the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool on 2 November, ending months of work to fix a failed blue chemical
articles.body: Donald Trump unveiled the completed repairs to the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool on 2 November, ending months of work to fix a failed blue chemical coating that had caused widespread algae growth. The project required workers to drain the 2,000-foot-long pool, remove the damaged coating and apply a new sealant. The work has drawn strong criticism after the cost rose to more than $14 million in federal contracts. This is far above the government's original estimate of less than $2 million. Speaking to people gathered at the National Mall, Trump praised the finished work and said the pool had been returned to its historic condition. "We took out the dirty water, we cleaned it up, and now it looks like crystal," Trump said during the ceremony. "It is back to the way Abraham Lincoln would have wanted it." The repairs follow years of problems with the pool's structure and appearance. Built in 1923, the pool holds more than 6.7 million gallons of water and is one of the most visited places in the US capital.A blue coating turned greenThe latest repairs were needed after a synthetic blue coating, added during an earlier maintenance project, started peeling away from the concrete floor. As the sealant broke down, it affected the pool's water circulation and created conditions that allowed algae to grow. By the middle of summer, the clear reflection of the Lincoln Memorial had been replaced by cloudy, bright green water. The National Park Service responded by closing parts of the area around the pool to visitors. Workers had to drain the entire pool, clean the concrete floor and apply a new sealant. The replacement coating has a neutral colour and is designed to handle high temperatures and strong sunlight. Federal contract records reviewed by reporters show that the cost of the work increased quickly. Contractors found additional problems with the underground pipes and water filtration pumps, adding to the total expense.Rising costs draw criticismThe growing cost of the project has become a major concern for government oversight groups and policy experts. A fact-check published by FactCheck.org in June 2026 found that Trump had repeatedly given higher-than-actual figures for previous spending on the pool when explaining the need for the latest contracts. In earlier public statements, Trump claimed that previous administrations had wasted more than $30 million on small repairs without fixing the algae problem. However, FactCheck.org found that total federal spending on the reflecting pool between 2010 and 2024 was about $34 million. This included a major $30.7 million reconstruction completed by the US Army Corps of Engineers in 2012. That project replaced the pool's original shallow foundation with deep concrete supports driven into the bedrock. The work was designed to stop the pool from sinking into the marshland underneath it. FactCheck.org reported that the latest maintenance work was first expected to cost less than $2 million. The money was meant to cover routine resurfacing and algae control. However, changes to the contracts later pushed the total value of government contracts for the current project above $14 million. The Guardian reported on 2 November 2026 that opposition lawmakers and public interest groups had criticised the rising costs. They pointed to the project as an example of poor control over government spending ahead of the upcoming midterm elections.A long history of maintenance problemsThe National Mall has faced long-running problems with maintaining its artificial pools and other water features. The 2012 reconstruction was designed to bring water directly from the Potomac River into the pool. It also included an advanced filtration system built underground. Despite these improvements, the pool suffered repeated outbreaks of toxic blue-green algae in 2017 and 2019. Both incidents required the pool to be drained completely. Each cleanup cost hundreds of thousands of dollars. Park Service officials said the pool's shallow depth, hot summer weather and large amounts of natural waste make it difficult to keep the water clear. Leaves, other organic material and waste from birds also add to the problem. "The reflecting pool is a massive, static body of water exposed to the elements," said National Park Service spokesperson Carol Johnson in a statement detailed in historical maintenance reports. "Keeping nearly seven million gallons of water pristine without over-using harsh chemicals requires constant mechanical balance."Political criticism ahead of the midtermsThe completion of the repairs comes as political activity increases across the country ahead of the US midterm elections. Trump's decision to hold an official ceremony at the monument attracted criticism from political opponents. They argued that the event was designed to highlight the administration's public works achievements while drawing attention away from the project's rising costs. The Guardian reported that administration officials defended the spending. They said the additional money was needed to fix poor work from earlier maintenance projects and provide a lasting solution for one of the National Mall's most important landmarks. The pool has now been filled with water again and reopened to the public. Automated filtration systems are operating around the clock to monitor the water and help prevent another outbreak of algae.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: 'Do you want Rahul vs PM Modi open debate?' Congress leader runs up public poll; asks BJP top brass to convince
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Lok Sabha leader of opposition Rahul Gandhi doubled down on his call for a debate with Prime Minister Narendra Modi over allegations of
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Lok Sabha leader of opposition Rahul Gandhi doubled down on his call for a debate with Prime Minister Narendra Modi over allegations of "foreign backing" levelled by both rival parties. His Congress and the BJP."Do you want to see a Rahul Gandhi vs Narendra Modi open debate?" the Congress leader wrote on X while posting a poll that contained two tricky options: "Yes, Modi Ji, Daro Mat" and "No, Modi Ji, Dar Gaye".The Congress leader, in a quirky note, also asked BJP's top brass, which includes some of PM Modi's colleagues in the Cabinet, to convince the Prime Minister to agree to a debate."Rajnath Singh Ji, Nitin Gadkari Ji, Shivraj Singh Chouhan Ji, Yogi Adityanath Ji, you you always have the PM’s best interest in mind, please convince him to come," the Congress scion quipped in the post.The Rae Bareli Lok Sabha MP posted the poll hours after he renewed his challenge to PM Modi to face him in an open debate, saying 24 hours had passed since he dared the PM.In a video shared on X, Rahul said, “24 hours have passed, Modi ji. I challenged you. You say that the opposition is anti-national. Pick any stage, any venue, and debate me.”“Who is the anti-national? Who has connections with foreign forces? And what kind of connections are they? Do it as soon as possible, don't be afraid,” he said.On Monday, Rahul had challenged the Prime Minister to an open debate on allegations of him becoming Prime Minister with "foreign help", saying the latter would not dare to accept it.The whole showdown began after Rahul retorted to Modi's 'Ekta Diwas' speech, in which the PM accused the opposition of turning into an "obstructionist force" (avrodh paksh).The Prime Minister also warned against forces "engaged in conspiracies to divide" the country, saying social media was "being weaponised, rumours being spread, and attempts being made to tarnish India's image"."When the country was seeking solutions to external challenges, some forces within the country were also creating instability by spreading lies and rumours. But the countrymen stood shoulder to shoulder with the nation," PM Modi said.“It is our misfortune that at this time in the country, the opposition has turned into an Avrodh Paksh rather than Virodh Paksh. In their frustration, these people are standing as obstacles in the way of the country’s development. This is not opposition; this is obstruction,” he added.In a veiled reference to Rahul's foreign trips, he said, “Due to the frustration of more than a decade, these people have now come out in the open. Who is secretly meeting whom abroad? Whom are the anti-India forces supporting? Who is speaking the language of India’s enemies? We will have to recognise all these patterns.”Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.
